1: In the lande of Hus there was a man whose name was Iob, & the same was a perfect and iust man, one that feared God and eschued euill
And he had seuen sonnes and three daughters

His substaunce also was seuen thousand sheepe, and three thousand camels, fiue hundred yoke of oxen, and fiue hundred shee asses, and a very great householde: so that he was one of the most principall men among all them of the east [countrey.
And his sonnes went and banquetted in their houses euery one his day, and sent for their three sisters to eate and drinke with them

And when the dayes of their banquetting were gone about, Iob sent and sanctified them, and gat vp early and offered for euery one a burnt offring: For Iob saide, It may be that my sonnes haue done some offence, & haue ben vnthankfull to God in their heartes. Thus did Iob euery day
And vpon a day when the children of God came and stoode before the lord, Satan came also among them
And the Lorde saide vnto Satan Whence comest thou? Satan aunswered the Lorde and saide: From compassing the earth to and fro, & from walking through it
And the Lorde saide vnto Satan: Hast thou not considered my seruaunt Iob, how there is none lyke him in the earth? a perfect and a iust man, one that feareth God, and eschueth euill
Satan aunswered, and saide vnto the Lorde: Doth Iob feare God for naught
Hast thou not preserued him and his house, and al that he hath on euery side? Thou hast blessed the worke of his handes, and his possession is encreased in the lande
But laye thyne hand now vpon him, and touche all that he hath, and he shall curse thee to thy face
And the Lorde saide vnto Satan: Lo, all that he hath be in thy power, only vpon him selfe see that thou lay not thine hand. And Satan went foorth from the presence of the Lorde
And vpon a certayne day, when his sonnes and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brothers house
There came a messenger vnto Iob, and sayde: The oxen were plowing and the asses feeding beside them
And the Sabees came violently, and toke them away, yea they haue slayne thy seruauntes with the edge of the sword: and I only am escaped alone to tell thee

While he was yet speaking, there came another, and sayde: The fire of God is fallen from heauen, and hath brent vp thy sheepe and seruauntes, and consumed them: and I only am escaped alone to tell thee

And whyle he was yet speaking there came another, and sayde: The Caldees made out their bandes, and fel vpon the camels, and haue caried them away, yea and slayne thy seruauntes with the sworde: and I only am gotten away alone to tell thee
And whyle he was yet speaking there came an other, and sayde: Thy sonnes and thy daughters were eating and drincking wine in their eldest brothers house

And behold there came a mightie great wind from beyond the wildernesse, and smote the foure corners of the house, whiche fell vpon thy children, and they are dead: and I am gotten away alone to tell thee
Then Iob stoode vp, and rent his clothes, & shaued his head, fell downe vpon the ground, worshipped
And sayde: Naked came I out of my mothers wombe, & naked shall I turne thyther againe: The Lorde gaue & the Lord hath taken away, blessed be the name of the Lorde
In all these thinges dyd Iob not offende, nor charged God foolishly
2: And on a day the children of God came and stoode before the Lorde, and Satan came also among the, and stoode before the Lorde
And the Lorde sayde vnto Satan: From whence commest thou? Satan aunswered the Lorde, and sayd: I haue gone about the lande, walked thorow it

And the Lorde sayde vnto Satan: Hast thou not considered my seruaunt Iob? howe there is none like vnto hym in the earth, a perfect and a iust man? one that feareth God, and eschueth euil, & continueth still in his vprightnesse, although thou mouedst me against hym, to destroy him without cause
And Satan aunswered the Lord, and sayd, Skinne for skinne, yea a man wil geue al that euer he hath for his life
But lay thyne hande nowe vpon hym, and touch [once] his bone and his fleshe, and he shall curse thee to thy face
And the Lord sayde vnto Satan: Lo, he is in thyne hand, but saue his lyfe
So went Satan foorth from the presence of the Lorde, and smote Iob with sore byles, from the sole of his foote vnto his crowne
And he toke a potsharde to scrape hym: and he sat downe among the asshes
Then sayd his wyfe vnto him: Doest thou continue yet in thy perfectnesse? curse God, and dye
But he sayde vnto her, Thou speakest like a foolish woman: shal we receaue good at the hande of God, and not receaue euyll? In all these thinges did not Iob sinne with his lippes

Nowe when Iobs three friendes heard of all the trouble that came vpon him, they came euery one fro his owne place [namely] Eliphas the Themanite, Bildad the Suhite, and Zophad the Naamathite: for they were agreed together to come to shewe their compassion vpon him, and to comfort hym
So when they lift vp their eyes a farre of, they knew him not: then they cryed and wept, and euery one of them rent his clothes, and sprinckled dust vpon their heades in the ayre
They sate them downe by him also vpon the grounde seuen dayes & seuen nightes, and none spake a worde vnto him: for they sawe that his greefe was very great
3: After this opened Iob his mouth, and cursed his day
And Iob aunswered, and sayde
Let the day perishe wherin I was borne, and the night in the whiche it was sayd, There is a man childe conceaued
The same day be [turned to] darknesse, and not regarded of God from aboue, neither let the light shyne vpon it
But let it be stayned with darknesse and the shadowe of death, let the [dimme] cloude fall vpon it, whiche may make it terrible as a most bitter day
Let the darke storme ouercome that night, and let it not be ioyned vnto the dayes of the yere, nor counted in the number of the monethes
Desolate be that night, and without gladnesse
Let them that curse the day, and that be redy to rayse vp mourning, geue it also their curse
Let the starres of that night be dimme thorowe darkenesse of it, let it loke for light, but haue none, neither let it see the dawning of the day
Because it shut not vp the doores of my mothers wombe, nor hyd sorowe from myne eyes
[Alas] why died I not in the birth? why dyd not I perishe assoone as I came out of [my mothers] wombe
Why set they me vpon their knees? why gaue they me sucke with their brestes
Then should I nowe haue lyen stil, I shoulde haue slept, and ben at rest
Lyke as the kinges and lordes of the earth, which haue buylded them selues speciall places
Or as the princes that haue had golde, and their houses full of siluer
Or [why] was not I hyd, as a thing borne out of tune, [either] as young children which neuer sawe the light
There must the wicked ceasse from their tyrannie, and there such as laboured valiauntly be at rest
There the prisoners rest together, they heare no more the voyce of the oppressour
There are small and great, and the seruaunt [is] free from his maister
Wherefore is the light geuen to hym that is in miserie? & lyfe vnto them that haue heauy heartes
Whiche long for death and finde it not, though they search more for it than for treasures
Which reioyce exceedingly, and be glad when they can finde the graue
From whom their endes are hyd, and consealed by God
For my sighes come before I eate, and my roringes are powred out like the water
For the thing that I feared is come vpon me, and the thing that I was afrayde of is happened vnto me
Was I not happy? Had I not quietnesse? Was I not in rest? And nowe commeth such miserie vpon me
4: And Eliphas the Themanite aunswered, & sayde
If we assay to come with thee, wilt thou be discontent? But who can withhold him selfe from speaking
Beholde, thou hast ben an instructer of many, & hast strenghtned the weery handes
Thy wordes haue set vp him that was falling, thou hast refreshed the weake knees
But nowe it is come vpon thee, and thou art greeued: it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled
Was not thy feare according to thy hope? and the perfectnesse of thy wayes according to thy expectation
Consider I pray thee who euer perished beyng an innocent? or when were the godly destroyed
For as I haue proued by experience, they that plow iniquitie & sow wretchednesse, reape the same
With the blast of God they perishe, with the breath of his nostrels are they consumed away
The roring of the lion, and the voyce of the lion, and the teeth of the lions whelpes are pulled out
The lion perisheth for lake of pray, & the lions whelpes are scattered abrode
But wheras a thing was hyd from me, yet myne care hath receaued a litle therof
In the thoughtes and visions of the night when sleepe commeth on men
Feare came vpon me & dread, which made all my bones to shake
The winde passed by before my presence, and made the heeres of my fleshe to stande vp
He stoode thereon and I knewe not his face, an image there was before myne eyes, and in the stilnesse hearde I a voyce
Shall man be more iust then God? or shall a man be purer then his maker
Beholde, he founde not trueth in his seruauntes, and in his angels there was folly
Howe much more in them that dwel in houses of clay, and whose foundation is but dust, which shall be consumed as it were with a moth
They shalbe smitten from the morning vnto the euening: yea they shall perishe for euer, when no man regardeth them
Is not their royaltie gone away with them? they shall dye truely, and not in wysdome
5: Crye I pray thee, if there be any that will aunswere thee, & loke thou vpon any of the holy
As for the foolish ma, wrathfulnesse killeth him, and enuie slayeth the ignorant
I haue seene my selfe when the foolish was deepe rooted, and sodenly I cursed his habitation
His children were without prosperitie, and they were slayne in the gate, and there was no man to deliuer them
His haruest was eaten of the hungrie, & taken from among the thornes, and the thurstie drunke vp their labour: It is not the earth that bringeth foorth iniquitie
Neither commeth sorowe out of the ground
But man is borne vnto labour, like as the sparkes flee vp [out of the hot coles,
But I woulde aske counsell at the Lorde, and talke with God
Whiche doth great thinges and vnsearcheable, [and] maruels without number
He geueth rayne vpon the earth, and powreth water vpon the streetes
To set vp them that be of lowe degree, and that those which are in heauinesse may be exalted to saluation
He destroyeth the deuices of the subtyll, so that their handes are not able to perfourme that which they do enterprise
He compasseth the wise in their owne craftinesse, & maketh foolishe the counsell of the wicked
They runne into darknesse by fayre day, and grope at the noone day as in the night
But he deliuereth the poore from the sworde, from their threatninges, and from the violence of the mightie
He is the hope of the poore, & the mouth of the wicked shalbe stopped
Behold, blessed is the man whom God correcteth, therefore refuse not thou the chastening of the almightie
For be maketh a wounde and he healeth: he smiteth, and his hande maketh whole againe
He shall deliuer thee in sixe troubles, & in the seuenth there shall no euil come to thee
In hunger he shall saue thee from death, and when it is warre, from the power of the sworde
Thou shalt be hyd from the scourge of the tongue, & when destruction commeth thou shalt not neede to feare
In destruction and dearth thou shalt be mery, and shalt not be afrayde of the beastes of the earth
For the stones of the land shalbe confederate with thee, and the beastes of the fielde shalbe at peace with thee
And thou shalt knowe that thy dwelling place shalbe in rest, and thou shalt visite thy habitation, & shalt not sinne
Thou shalt see also that thy seede shall be great, and thy posteritie as the grasse vpon the earth
Thou shalt come also to thy graue in a full age, like a corne sheafe cut downe in due season
Lo, this we our selues haue proued by experience, and euen thus it is: Hearken thou to it also, that thou mayest take heede to thy selfe
6: But Iob aunswered, and sayde
O that my complaynt were truely wayed, and my punishment layde in the balaunces together
For nowe it woulde be heauier then the sande of the sea: and this is the cause, that my wordes fayle me
For the arrowes of the almightie are vpon me, the poyson therof hath drunke vp my spirite, and the terrible feares of God are set against me
Doth the wild asse rore when he hath grasse? or loweth the oxe when he hath fodder [inough
That which is vnsauerie, shall it be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the whyte of an egge
The thinges that sometime I might not away withel, are nowe my meate for very sorowe
O that I might haue my desire, and that God woulde graunt me the thing that I long for
O that God would begin and smite me, that he would let his hand go and take me cleane away
Then shoulde I haue some comfort, yea I woulde desire him in my payne that he would not spare, for I wil not be against the wordes of the holy one
For what powre haue I to endure? And what is myne end, that my soule might be patient
Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my fleshe of brasse
Is it not so that there is in me no helpe? & that my substaunce is taken from me
He that is in tribulation, ought to be comforted of his neyghbour: but the feare of the almightie is cleane away
Myne owne brethren passe ouer by me as the water brooke, & as the ouerflowing of waters, whiche do hastly go away
Whiche are blackish be reason of the ice, and wherin the snowe is hyd
Which when they haue passed by do vanishe, and when the heate commeth they fayle out of their place
They depart from the course of their wonted chanell to other places, they runne in vayne and perishe
They that went to The man considered them, and they that went to Saba wayted for them
But they were confounded in their hope, they came thyther and were ashamed
Euen such truely are ye, nowe that ye see my miserie ye are afrayde
Did I desire you to bring vnto me, or to geue me any of your substaunce
To deliuer me from the enemies hand, or to saue me from the hande of the tyrauntes
Teache me, and I will hold my tong: and wherin I haue erred; cause me to vnderstande
How strong are the wordes of trueth? and which of you can rebuke or reproue them
Do ye imagine to reproue wordes, that the talke of the afflicted shoulde be as the winde
Ye fall vpon the fatherlesse, and digge a pit to ouerthrowe your owne frende
And therfore be content, & loke now vpon me, and I will not lye before your face
Turne I pray you, be indifferent iudges: turne agayne, and ye shall see myne vngiltinesse
whether there be any vnrighteousnes in my tongue, or vayne wordes in my mouth
7: Is ther not an appoynted time to man vpon earth? Are not his dayes also like the dayes of an hired seruaunt
For like as a bonde seruaunt desireth the shadowe, and as an hyreling woulde fayne haue the rewarde of his worke
Euen so haue I laboured whole monethes long in vayne, and many a carefull night haue I tolde
When I layde me downe to sleepe, I sayde, O when shall I arise? and measuring the euening, I am euen full with tossing to and fro vnto the dawning of the day
My fleshe is clothed with wormes and dust of the earth: my skinne is withered and become horrible
My dayes passe ouer more spedyly then a weauers shuttle, and are spent without hope
O remember that my lyfe is but a winde, and that myne eye shall no more see pleasures
Yea and the eye that hath seene me, shal see me no more: for yer thou fasten thyne eye vpon me, I come to naught
The cloude is consumed and vanished away: so he that goeth downe to the graue shall come no more vp
Nor turne againe into his house, neither shall his place knowe him any more
Therfore I wil not spare my mouth, but I will speake in the trouble of my spirite, and muse in the bitternesse of my mynde
Am I a sea or a whale fish, that thou kepest me [so] in prison
When I say, My bed shal comfort me, I shall haue some refreshing by talking to my selfe vpon my couch
Then fearest thou me with dreames, & makest me so afrayde through visions
That my soule wisheth rather to perishe and die, then my bones to remayne
I can see no remedy, I shall liue no more: O spare me then, for my dayes are but vanitie
What is man that thou doest magnifie him? and that thou settest thy heart vpon him
Thou visitest him early and euery day, euery moment doest thou trie him
Why goest thou not fro me, nor lettest me alone, so long till I may swalowe downe my spyttle
I haue offended, what shall I do vnto the, O thou preseruer of men? Why hast thou set me [as a marke] against thee, so that I am a burden to my selfe
Why doest thou not pardon my trespasses, and take away myne iniquitie? Behold, nowe must I sleepe in the dust, and if thou sekest me to morowe in the morning, I shal not be
8: Then aunswered Bildad the Suhite, & said
Howe long wilt thou talke of such thinges? howe long shall the wordes of thy mouth be as a mightie wind
Doth God paruert the thing that is lawfull? or doth the almightie destroy the thing that is right
For seyng that thy sonnes sinned against him, did not he send them into the place of their iniquitie
If thou wouldest nowe resorte vnto God be times, and make thy prayer to the almightie
If thou wouldest liue a pure and godly life: shoulde he not awake vp vnto thee immediatly, and make the habitation of thy righteousnesse prosperous
In so much that wherin so euer thou haddest litle afore, thou shouldest haue nowe great aboundaunce
Enquire I pray thee of the former age, and search diligently among their fathers
(For we are but of yesterday, and consider not that our dayes vpon earth are but a shadowe.
Shall not they shew thee, and tel thee, yea and gladly confesse the same, and vtter the wordes of their heart
May a rushe be greene without moystnesse? or may the grasse growe without water
No, but whilste it is nowe in his greennesse, though it be not cut downe, yet withereth it before any other hearbe
So are the pathes of al that forget God, and the hypocrites hope shall come to naught
His confidence shalbe destroyed, and his trust shalbe a spiders webbe
He shal leane vpon his house, but it shal not stande: he shall holde him fast by it, yet shall it not endure
It is a greene [tree] before the sunne, & shooteth foorth the braunches ouer his garden
The rootes thereof are wrapped about the fountayne, and are folden about the house of stones
If any plucke it from his place, and it denie, saying, I haue not seene thee
Behold it will reioyce by this meanes, if it may growe in another mould
Beholde, God will not cast away a vertuous man, neither wil he helpe the vngodly
Thy mouth shall he fill with laughing, and thy lippes with gladnesse
They also that hate thee shalbe clothed with shame, & the dwelling of the vngodly shall come to naught
9: Iob aunswered, and sayde
I knowe it is so of a trueth: For how may a man [compared] vnto God be iustified
If he wil argue with hym, he can not aunswere hym one thing of a thousande
He is wyse in heart and mightie in strength: who hath ben fearce against hym, and hath prospered
He translateth the mountaynes, or euer they be aware it is he that ouerthroweth them in his wrath
He remoueth the earth out of her place, that the pillers therof shake withall
He commaundeth the sunne, and it ryseth not: he closeth vp the starres as vnder a signet
He hym selfe alone spreadeth out the heauens, and goeth vpon the waues of the sea
He maketh the Waynes of heauen, the Orion, the seuen starres, and the secret places of the south
He doth great thinges & vnsearcheable, yea and wonders without number
Lo, when he goeth by me, I shal not see hym, and when he passeth, I shall not perceaue hym
If he be hastie to take away, who wil make him restore it? or who will say vnto hym, what doest thou
God will not withdraw his anger, and the most mightie helpes do stowpe vnder hym
Howe much lesse shall I aunswere him? or howe shoulde I finde out my wordes with him
For though I were righteous, yet might I not geue him one word againe, but mekely submit my selfe to hym as my iudge
If I had called vpon hym, and he had aunswered me, yet woulde I not beleue that he hearde my voyce
He troubleth me so with the tempest, and woundeth me out of measure without a cause
He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitternesse
If [men will speake] of strength, lo he is strong: if [men will speake] of iudgement, who shall bring me in to pleade
If I will iustifie my selfe, myne owne mouth shall condempne me: if I will [put foorth my selfe for] a perfect man, he shall proue me a wicked doer
For though I be an innocent and my conscience cleare, yet am I weery of my lyfe
This is one poynt, and therefore I sayd, He destroyeth both the perfect and vngodly
And though he slay sodaynly with the scourge, yet will he laugh at the punishment of the innocent
As for the worlde it is geuen ouer into the hande of the wicked, and he shall couer the faces of the iudges therof: if not, where is he, or who is he [that can shewe the contrarie?
My dayes are more swyft then a runner, they are gone & haue seene no good thing
They are passed away as the shippes that be good vnder sayle, & as the eagle that fleeth to the pray
If I say, I will forget my complayning, I will ceasse from my wrath, and comfort my selfe
Then am I afrayde of all my sorowes, for I knowe that thou wilt not iudge me innocent
If I be wicked, why then labour I in vayne
If I washe my selfe with snowe water, and make myne handes neuer so cleane at the well
Yet shalt thou dippe me in the myre, and mine owne clothes shal defile me
For he that I must geue aunswere vnto, and with whom I go to the lawe, is not a man as I am
Neither is there any dayesman to lay his hande betweene vs
Let hym take his rodde away from me, yea let hym make me no more afrayde of him
And then shall I aunswere hym without any feare: but because I am not so, I holde me still
10: My soule is cut of though I lyue, I wil powre out my coplaynte against my selfe, and will speake out of the very heauinesse of my soule
I will say vnto God: O do not condempne me, but shewe me wherefore thou contendest so with me
Thinkest thou it welldone to oppresse me? to cast me of beyng the workes of thy handes? and to mayntayne the counsell of the vngodly
Hast thou fleshy eyes? or doest thou loke as a man loketh
Or are thy dayes as the dayes of man? and thy yeres as mans yeres
That thou makest such inquisition for my wickednes, and searchest out my sinne
Whereas thou knowest whether I shall do wickedly or no, and that none can deliuer me out of thyne hande
Thy handes haue made me, & fashioned me altogether rounde about, wilt thou then destroy me
Remember I besech thee that thou madest me as the moulde of the earth, and shalt bring me into dust againe
Hast thou not powred me as it were milke, & turned me to cruddes like cheese
Thou hast couered me with skinne and fleshe, and ioyned me together with bones and sinnowes
Thou hast graunted me life, and done me good: and thy visitation hath preserued my spirite
Thou hast hyd these thinges in thyne heart [yet] I am sure that thou remembrest this thing
If I dyd sinne, thou haddest an eye vnto me, and shalt not pronounce me innocent from myne offence
If I haue done wickedly, wo is me therefore: If I haue done righteously, yet dare I not lift vp my head, so full am I of confusion, and see myne owne miserie
And let it increase, hunte me as a lion, & returne and shew thy selfe maruaylous vpon me
Thou bringest freshe witnesse against me, and thy wrath increasest thou vpon me: diuers and many are the plagues that I am in
Wherfore hast thou brought me out of the wombe? O that I had perished, and that no eye had seene me
And that I were as though I had not ben, but brought from the wombe to the graue
Are not my dayes fewe? Let him then leaue of fro me, and let me a lone, that I may comfort my selfe a litle
Afore I go [thyther from whence] I shall not turne againe, euen to the lande of darknesse and shadowe of death
Yea a lande as darke as darknesse it selfe, and into the shadowe of death where is none order, but the light is there as darknesse
11: Then aunswered Sophar the Naamathite, and sayde
Shoulde not [he that maketh] many wordes be aunswered? Shoulde he that bableth much be commended therin
Shoulde thy lies make men holde their peace, and when thou mockest [others] shall no man make thee ashamed
For thou hast sayde, my doctrine is pure, and I am cleane in thyne eyes
But O that God woulde speake, and open his lippes against thee
That he might shewe thee the secretes of wysdome, howe thou hast deserued double according to right: Know therfore that God hath forgotten thee for thyne iniquitie
Art thou able to finde out [the secretes of] God? Or wilt thou attayne to the perfectnesse of the almightie
It is hier then heauen, what art thou able to do? deeper then the hel, how wilt thou then knowe it
The measure of it is longer then the earth, and broder then the sea
Though he turne all thinges vpsyde downe, close them in, gather them together, who will turne hym from his purpose
For it is he that knoweth vayne men, he seeth their wickednesse also, shoulde he not then consider it
Yet vayne man would be wyse, though man [newe] borne is lyke a wilde asses coulte
If thou preparedst thyne heart, and liftedst vp thyne handes towarde hym
If thou wouldest put away the wickednes whiche thou hast in hande, so that no vngodlinesse dwell in thy house
Then mightest thou lift vp thy face without shame, & then shouldest thou be sure and haue no neede to feare
Then shouldest thou forget thy miserie, and thinke no more vpon it, then vpon the waters that runne by
Then should thy lyfe be as cleare as the noone day, thou shouldest shine forth, and be as the morning
Then mightest thou be bolde because there is hope, and take thy rest quietly, as compassed with a trenche
Then mightest thou lye downe and none to make thee afrayde, yea many one should make suite vnto thee
As for the eyes of the vngodly they shall faile, and they shal not escape: and their hope shalbe sorowe of minde
12: So Iob aunswered, & saide
Then no doubt ye are the men alone, and wysdome shall perishe with you
But I haue vnderstanding aswell as ye, and am not inferior to you: Yea who knoweth not these thinges
I am as one mocked of his neighbour, who calleth vpon God, & he heareth him: The iust & the vpright is laughed to scorne
Being as alight despised in the heartes of the riche, and as one redy to fall
The houses of robbers are in wealth and prosperitie, and they that maliciouslie meddle against God dwell without care, in those thinges that God hath geuen richely with his hande
Aske the cattaile, and they shall enfourme thee: the foules of the ayre, and they shall tell thee
Or the encrease of the earth, and it shall shew thee: or the fishes of the sea, and they shall certifie thee
What is he but he knoweth that the hande of the Lorde made all these
In whose hande is the soule of euery liuing thing, and the breath of all mankinde
Haue not the eares pleasure in hearing? and the mouth in tasting the thing that it eateth
Among olde persons there is wysedome, and in age is vnderstanding
Yea, with [God] is wysdome and strength, it is he that hath counsell and foreknowledge
Beholde if he breake downe a thing, who can set it vp againe? yf he shut a thing, who wyll open it
Beholde, if he withholde the waters, they drye vp: yf he let them go, they destroy the earth
With him is strength and wysdome: both the deceauer and he that is deceaued are his
He carieth away the wyse men as it were a spoyle, and bringeth the iudges out of their wittes
He taketh away the subiection of the people from their kinges, and girdeth their loynes with a bonde
He leadeth away the great men into captiuitie, and turneth the mightie vpside downe
He stoppeth the mouth of them that speake trueth, & disapoynteth the aged of their reason
He powreth contempt vpon princes, and maketh the strength of the mightie weake
Loke what lyeth hid in darkenesse he declareth it openly, and the very shadowe of death bringeth he to light
He [both] increaseth the people and destroyeth them, he maketh them to multiplie, and diminisheth them
He taketh away the hearte of them that be heades of ye people of the earth, and causeth them to wander in the wildernesse out of the way
They grope in the darke without light, and he maketh them to stacker like a drunken man
13: Lo, all [this] haue I seene with mine eye, heard with mine eare, and vnderstande it
What ye knowe, that same do I know also, neither am I inferior vnto you
Neuerthelesse, I talke with the almightie, and my desire is to commune with God
As for you, ye are workmaisters of lyes, and vnprofitable phisitians altogether
Woulde God ye kept your tongue, for then might ye be taken for wise men
Now heare my reasoning, and ponder the argument of my lippes
Wyll you speake wickedlie for gods [defence] and talke deceitfully for his [cause?
Wyll ye accept the person of him? or wyll ye contende for God
Shall that helpe you when he calleth you to reckening? For as one man mocketh an other, so do ye mocke him
He shall punishe you, and reproue you, if ye do secretly accept any person
Shall not his excellencie make you afrayde? Shall not his terrible feare fall vpon you
Your remembraunce is lyke vnto a sparke, and your bodies lyke the claye
Holde your tongues for my sake, that I also may speake, and my sorowe shalbe the lesse
Wherefore do I beare my fleshe in my teeth, and put my soule in myne handes
Lo, though he slay me, yet wyl I trust in him: but I wyll reproue myne owne wayes in his sight
He shalbe my saluation: for there may no hypocrite come before him
Heare diligently my wordes, and ponder my sayinges with your eares
Beholde, now haue I prepared my iudgement, and knowe that I shalbe founde righteous
What is he that wyll go to lawe with me? if I now holde my tongue I dye
Neuerthelesse, graunt me two thinges, and then wyll I not hide my selfe from thee
Withdrawe thyne hande from me, and let not the fearefull dreade of thee make me afrayde
Then call, and I wyll aunswere: or let me speake, and geue me then an aunswere
How many are my misdeedes and sinnes? let me knowe my transgressions and offences
Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thyne enemie
Wylt thou breake a leafe driuen to and fro, and wilt thou pursue the drye stubble
For thou layest sharply to my charge, and punishest me for the sinnes of my youth
Thou puttest my feete also in the stockes, and lokest narowly vnto all my pathes, and makest the print thereof in the heeles of my feete
And I as a rotten thing do consume away, as a garment that is moth eaten
14: Man that is borne of woman, hath but a short time to lyue, and is full of miserie
He commeth vp, and is cut downe like a floure: He fleeth as it were a shadow, and neuer continueth in one state
Doest thou open thyne eyes vpon such one, and bringest me into thy iudgement
Who can make it cleane that commeth of an vncleane thing? no bodye
The dayes of man surely are determined, the number of his monethes are knowen onely vnto thee, thou hast appoynted him his bondes which he can not go beyonde
Go from him, that he may rest vntill his day come which he loketh for, lyke as an hireling doth
For if a tree be cut downe, there is some hope yet that it wyll sproute and shoote foorth the braunches againe
Though the roote of it be waxen olde, and the stocke thereof be dead in the grounde
Yet when it getteth the sent of water, it wyll budde and bring foorth bowes, lyke as a tree that is planted
But as for man, when he is dead, perished, and consumed away, what becommeth of him
As the waters passe from the sea, and as the flood decayeth and dryeth vp
So man after he is asleepe ryseth not, he shall not wake tyll the heauens be no more, nor rise out of his sleepe
O that thou wouldest hide me in the graue, & keepe me secret vntyl thy wrath were past, and to appoynt me a time wherein thou mightest remember me
May a dead man lyue againe? All the dayes of my lyfe wyll I wayte still, till my chaunging shall come
Thou shalt call [me] and I shall aunswere thee, despise not thou the worke of thyne owne handes
For now thou numbrest all my goinges, and geuest no delay vnto my sinne
Myne iniquitie is sealed vp as it were in a bagge, and thou addest [punishement] vnto my wickednesse
The mountaines fal away at the last, the rockes are remoued out of their place
The waters pearse through the very stones by litle & litle, the floodes washe away the grauell and earth: so shalt thou destroy the hope of man
Thou preuaylest still against him, so that he passeth away: thou chaungest his estate and puttest him from thee
And whether his children come to worship or no, he can not tell: And if they be men of lowe degree, he knoweth not
But while his fleshe is vpon him, it must haue sorowe: and his soule shall mourne within him
15: Then aunswered Eliphaz the Themanite, and saide
Shall a wyse mans aunswere be as the winde, and fill a mans belly as it were with the winde of the east
Shall he reproue with a worde that is nothing worth, & speake the thinges which can do no good
Surely thou hast cast of feare, and restrainest prayer before God
For thy mouth setteth forth thyne owne iniquitie, seeing thou hast chosen the tongue of the craftie
Thyne owne mouth condempneth thee, and not I: yea, thyne owne lippes shape an aunswere against thee
Art thou the first man that euer was borne? or wast thou made before the hils
Hast thou heard the secret counsell of God? and doest thou restraine wysdome to thee
What knowest thou, that we knowe not? And what vnderstandest thou, but we can the same
With vs are both olde and aged men, yea such as haue liued longer then thy father
Thinkest thou it a small thing of the consolations of God? with thee is a lying worde
Why doth thyne heart so bewitche thee? And wherefore winckest thou with thyne eyes
That thy minde is so pufte vp against God, and lettest such wordes go out of thy mouth
What is man, that he should be cleane? and he which is borne of a woman, whereby he might be righteous
Beholde he doth not trust his sainctes, yea, the very heauens are not cleane in his sight
How much more then an abhominable and vyle man, which drincketh wickednesse like water
I will tel thee, heare me, and I will shewe thee that I haue seene
Which wyse men haue tolde, and haue not hid that which they receaued from theyr fathers
Unto whom alone the earth was geue, and no straunger went among them
The vngodly soroweth all the dayes of his lyfe as it were a woman with childe, and the number of a tirauntes yeres is vnknowen
A feareful sounde is [euer] in his eares, and when he is in peace, the destroyer shall come vpon him
He beleueth neuer to be deliuered out of darknesse: for the sworde is alwayes before his eyes
He wandreth abrode for bread where it is, knowing that the day of darkenesse is redie at his hande
Trouble and anguishe wil make him afrayde, and compasse him about, as is a king in the middest of an armie
For he hath stretched out his hande against God, and armed him selfe against the almightie
He runneth proudly vpon him, & with a stiffe necke fighteth he against him
Where as he couereth his face with fatnesse, and maketh his body well lyking
Therefore shall his dwelling be in desolate cities, and in houses which no man inhabiteth, but are become heapes of stones
He shall not be riche, neither shall his substaunce continue, neither shal the prosperitie thereof be prolonged vpon earth
He shall neuer depart out of darkenesse, the flame shal drye vp his branches, with the blast of ye mouth [of God] shall he be taken away
He beleeueth not that he erreth in vanitie, and yet vanitie shalbe his recompence
He shal perishe afore his time be worne out, and his braunche shall not be greene
He shalbe plucked of as an vntimely grape from the vine, and shall let his floure fall as the oliue doth
For the congregation of hypocrites shalbe desolate, and the fire shall consume the houses of such as are greedie to receaue giftes
He conceaueth trauaile, and beareth vanitie, and their body bringeth foorth disceyte
16: Iob aunswered, & saide
I haue oft times heard such thinges: miserable geuers of comfort are ye all the sort of you
Shall not vaine wordes come yet to an ende? Or what maketh thee bolde so to aunswere
I coulde speake as ye do also: but would God that your soule were in my soules steade, then could I frame wordes for you, and shake my head at you
I shoulde comfort you with my mouth, & releasse your paine with the talking of my lippes
For all my wordes my sorowe wyll not ceasse: And though I holde my tongue, what am I eased
But now that [God] hath sent me aduersitie, thou hast troubled al my congregation
And that thou hast filled me with wrinckles my fleshe is recorde, and my leanenesse ryseth vp against me and beareth witnes thereof in my face
His wrath hath torne [me] he hateth me, & gnasheth vpon me with his teeth: myne enemie loketh fiercely vpon me with his eyes
They haue opened their mouthes wide vpon me, and smitten me vpon the cheeke dispitefully, they gather the selues together against me
God hath shut me vp with the vngodly, and deliuered me into the handes of the wicked
I was in wealth, but he hath brought me to nought: he hath taken me by the necke, he hath all to shaken me, and set me as a marke for him selfe
His archers compasse me rounde about, he woundeth my raines, and doth not spare, my bowels hath he powred vpon the grounde
He hath geuen me one wounde vpon an other, and is fallen vpon me lyke a giaunt
I haue sowed a sackecloth vpon my skinne, and wallowed my head in the dust
My face is withered with weeping, & in mine eyes is the shadowe of death
Howbeit there is no wickednesse in my handes, but my prayer is cleane
O earth couer not thou my blood, and let my crying finde no roome
For lo, my witnesse is in heauen, and he that knoweth me, is in the height
My friendes geue me many wordes to scorne, and myne eye powreth out teares vnto God
O that a body might pleate with God, as one man doth with an other
Yet the number of my yeres is come, and the way that I must go is at hand, from whence I shall not turne againe
17: My breath is corrupt, my dayes are shortened, I am harde at deathes doore
Froward men are with me, and myne eye must continue in the bitternesse of them
O deliuer me, and loke out one to be my suretie in thy sight: what is he that knoweth who wyll promise for me
For thou hast withholden their heartes from vnderstanding, therefore shalt thou not set [them] vp on hie
He that speaketh flatterie to his friend, the eyes of his children shall fayle
He hath made me a byworde of the people, where as afore I was their ioy
Myne eye is dimme for very heauinesse, and all my strength is lyke a shadowe
Vertuous men therefore shall well consider this, and the innocent shal take part against the hypocrite
The righteous also wyll kepe his way, and he that hath cleane handes wyll euer be stronger and stronger
As for al you, turne you and get you hence [I pray you] seeing I can not finde one wyse man among you
My dayes are past, and my counsailes and thoughtes of my heart are vanished away
Chaunging the night into day, and the light approching into darkenesse
Though I tary neuer so much, yet the graue is my house, & I haue made my bed in the darke
I saide to corruption, thou art my father, and to the wormes, you are my mother and my sister
Where is then now my hope? or who hath considered the thing that I loke for
These shall go downe with me into the pit, and lye with me in the dust
18: Then aunswered Bildad the Suhite, and saide
When wyll ye make an ende of your wordes? Marke well, and then we wyll speake
Wherfore are we counted as beastes, and reputed so vyle in your sight
He destroyeth him selfe with his anger: Shall the earth be forsaken, or any stone remoued out of his place because of thee
Yea, the light of the vngodly shalbe put out, and the sparke of his fire shall not shine
The light shall be darke in his dwelling, and his candle shall be put out with him
The steppes of his strength shalbe restrayned, and his owne counsaile shall cast him downe
For his feete are taken [as it were] in the net, & he walketh vpon the snares
The grinne shall take him by the heele, and it shall catche him that is thirstie of blood
The snare is layde for him in the grounde, and a pitfall in the way
Fearefulnesse shall make him afraide on euery side, and shall driue him to his feete
Hunger shalbe his strength, and destruction shalbe redye at his side
It shall eate the strength of his owne skinne, euen the first borne of death shall eate his strength
His hope shalbe rooted out of his dwelling, and shall bring him to the king of feare
Other men shall dwell in his house, and it shalbe none of his, and brimstone shall be scattered vpon his habitation
His rootes shalbe dryed vp beneath, and aboue shall his braunche be cut downe
His remembraunce shall perishe from the earth, and he shall haue no name in the streete
They shall driue him from the light into darkenesse, and chaste him cleane out of the worlde
He shall neither haue children nor kinsfolkes among his people, no nor any posteritie in his dwellinges
They that come after him, shalbe astonyed at his day, and they that go before shalbe afrayde
Such are now the dwellinges of the wicked, and this is the place of him that knoweth not God
19: Iob aunswered, and saide
How long wyll ye vexe my soule, and trouble me with wordes
Lo, ten times haue ye reproched me, and are not ashamed, but haue laughed me to scorne
Be it that I haue erred in deede, myne errour then remaineth with my selfe
But if ye wyll aduaunce your selues against me, and rebuke me for the shame that is come vpon me
Know this then, that it is God which hath ouerthrowe me, and hath compassed me with his net
If I complaine of the violence that is done vnto me, I cannot be heard: and if I crye, there is no sentence geuen with me
He hath hedged vp my way that I can not passe, and he hath set darkenesse in my pathes
He hath spoyled me of myne honour, and taken the crowne away from my head
He hath destroyed me on euery side and I am gone: my hope hath he taken away as a tree pluckt vp by the roote
His wrath is kindled against me, he taketh me as though I were his enemie
His men of warre come together, which made their way ouer me, and besieged my dwelling rounde about
He hath put my brethren farre away from me, and myne acquaintaunce are also become straungers vnto me
Myne owne kinsefolkes haue forsaken me, and my best acquainted haue forgotten me
The seruauntes and maydens of myne owne house toke me for a straunger, and I am become as an aliaunt in their sight
I called my seruaunt, and he gaue me no aunswere: [no though] I prayed him with my mouth
Myne owne wyfe might not abyde my breath, though I prayed her for the children sake of myne owne body
Yea, the young men despised me, and when I rose they spake euill vpon me
All my most familiers abhorred me: and they whom I loued best, are turned against me
My bone cleaueth to my skinne and to my fleshe, onely there is left me the skinne about my teeth
Haue pitie vpon me, haue pitie vpon me, O ye my friendes, for the hande of God hath touched me
Why do ye persecute me as God [doth] and are not satisfied with my fleshe
O that my wordes were now written, O that they were put in a booke
And grauen with an iron penne in leade, or in stone, to continue
For I am sure that my redeemer saueth, and he shall rayse vp at the latter day them that lye in the dust
And though after my skinne the [wormes] destroy this body, yet shall I see God in my fleshe
Whom I my selfe shall see, and myne eyes shall beholde, and none other for me, though my raines are consumed within me
But ye saide, why is he persecuted? and there was a deepe matter in me
But beware of the sworde: for the sword wylbe auenged of wickednesse, and be sure that there is a iudgement
20: Then aunswered Sophar the Naamathite, and saide
For the same cause do my thoughtes compell me to aunswere, and therefore, make haste
I haue sufficiently heard the checking of my reproofe, therefore the spirite of myne vnderstanding causeth me to aunswere
Knowest thou not this of olde, and since God plaged man vpon earth
That the gladnesse of the vngodlie hath ben short, and that the ioy of hypocrites continued but the twinckling of an eye
Though he be magnified vp to the heauen, so that his head reacheth vnto the cloudes
Yet at a turne he perisheth for euer, insomuch that they which haue seene him, shall say, Where is he
He shall vanishe as a dreame, so that he can no more be founde, and shal passe away as a vision in the night
So that the eye which sawe him before, shal haue no more sight of him, and his place shall know him no more
His children shalbe faine to agree with the poore, and his handes shall restore their goodes
From his youth his bones are full of pleasures, but now shall it lye downe within him in the earth
When wickednesse was sweete in his mouth, he hyd it vnder his tongue
That he fauoured, that would he not forsake, but kept it close in his throte
The bread that he did eate, is turned to the poyson of serpentes within his bodye
The riches that he deuoured shall he parbreake againe: for God shall drawe them out of his belly
He shall sucke the gall of serpentes, and the adders tongue shall slay him
So that he shall no more see the ryuers and brookes of hony and butter
The thing he hath laboured for, shall he restore, and shall not eate of it: great trauaile shall he make for riches, but he shall not enioy them
And why? he hath oppressed the poore, and not helped them: houses hath he spoyled, and not builded them
Because he could not perceaue when his belly was well, through his greedie desire he shall not escape
There shall none of his meate be left, therefore shall no man loke for his goodes
When he had plenteousnesse of euery thing, yet was he poore, though he was helped on euery side
And it shall come to passe, that wherewith he purposed to fill his belly, God shall powre the furie of his wrath theron, and shall cause his indignation to raigne vpon him, and vpon his meate
He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bowe of steele shall strike him through
The [arowe] is taken foorth and gone out of the quiuer, and a glistering sword through the gall of him: so feare shall come vpon him
All darknesse shalbe hid in their secrete places, an vnkindled fire shal consume him: and loke what remaineth in his house, it shalbe destroyed
The heauen shal declare his wickednesse, and the earth shall take part against him
The substaunce that he hath in his house, shalbe taken away and perishe in the day of the Lordes wrath
This is the portion that the wicked man shal haue of God, and the heritage that he may loke for of God, because of his wordes
21: Iob aunswered, and saide
O heare diligently my wordes, and that shalbe in steede of your consolations
Suffer me that I may speake, and when I haue spoken mocke on
Is it for mans sake that I make this disputation? Which if it were so, shoulde not my spirite then be in sore trouble
Marke me [well] and be abashed, and lay your hande vpon your mouth
For when I consider [my selfe] I am afrayde, and my fleshe is smitten with feare
Wherefore do wicked men liue, come to their olde age, and increase in richesse
Their children lyue in their sight, and their generation before their eyes
Their houses are safe from all feare, and the rod of God is not vpon them
Their bullocke gendreth and that not out of time, their cowe calueth and is not vnfruitfull
They sende foorth their children by flockes, & their sonnes [leade the] daunce
They beare with them tabrets and harpes, and reioyce in the sounde of the organs
They spend their dayes in wealthines, but sodainely they go downe to the graue
They say also vnto God: Go from vs, we desire not the knowledge of thy wayes
Who is the almightie that we should serue him? And what profite should we haue if we should pray vnto him
Lo, there is vtterly no goodnesse in their hande, therefore wyll I not haue to do with the counsaile of the vngodly
How oft shall the candell of the wicked be put out, and their destruction come vpon them? O what sorowe shall God geue them for their part in his wrath
Yea, they shalbe euen as hay before the winde, and as chaffe that the storme carieth away
God wyll lay vp the sorowe of the father for his children: & when he rewardeth him, he shall know it
Their owne miserie shal they see with their eyes, and drinke of the fearefull wrath of the almightie
For what careth he for his house after his death, when the number of his monethes is cut short
Seeing God hath the highest power of all, who can teache him any knowledge
One dyeth in his full strength, being in all ease and prosperitie
His breastes are full of milke, and his bones runne full of marowe
Another dyeth in the bitternes of his soule, and neuer eateth with pleasure
They shall sleepe both alyke in the earth, and the wormes shall couer them
Beholde, I know what ye thinke, yea and the subtiltie that ye imagine against me
For ye say where is the princes palace? and where is the dwelling of the vngodly
Haue ye not asked them that go by the way? Doubtlesse ye cannot denie their tokens
That the wicked is kept vnto the day of destruction, and the vngodly shalbe brought foorth to the day of wrath
Who dare declare his way to his face? who wil rewarde him for that he doth
Yet shall he be brought to his graue, and dwell among the heape [of the dead.
Then shal the slymie valley be sweet vnto him, all men also must folowe him, as there are innumerable gone before him
Howe vayne then is the comfort that ye geue me, seyng falshood remayneth in all your aunsweres
22: So Eliphas the Themanite gaue aunswere, and sayde
May a man be profitable vnto God, as he that is wise may be profitable vnto him selfe
Is it any aduauntage to the almightie that thou art righteous? or shall it profite him that thou makest thy wayes perfect
Is he afrayde to reproue thee, and to step foorth with thee into iudgement
Is not thy wickednesse great, and thy vngratious deedes innumerable
For thou hast taken the pledge from thy brother for naught, and robbed the naked of their clothing
To such as were weery, hast thou geuen no water to drinke, & hast withdrawen bread from the hungrie
But the mightie man had the earth, and he that was in auctoritie dwelt in it
Thou hast sent wydowes away emptie, and the armes of the fatherlesse were broken
Therefore art thou compassed about with snares, & sodenly vexed with feare
Shouldest thou then see no darknesse? shoulde not the water fludde run ouer thee
Is not God on high in the heauen? beholde the heyght of the starres how hie they are
Wilt thou therfore say, Tushe, howe should God know? can he iudge through the darke cloude
Tushe, the cloudes couer him that he may not see, and he walketh on the top of heauen
Hast thou marked the way of the world, wherin wicked men haue walked
Whiche were cut downe out of time, and whose foundation was as an ouerflowing ryuer
Whiche sayd vnto God, Go from vs: and asked what the almightie coulde do for them
He filled their houses with good things: but the counsell of the vngodly be farre from me
The righteous sawe it and were glad, and the innocent laughed them to scorne
Is our substaunce bewen downe? As for the remnaunt of them the fire hath consumed
Therefore reconcile thee vnto God, and be at peace: so shall all thinges prospere with thee right well
Receaue I pray thee the lawe at his mouth, and lay vp his wordes in thyne heart
For if thou wilt turne to the almightie, thou shalt be buyld vp, and put all vnrighteousnes from thy dwelling
Thou shalt lay vp golde [as plentyful] as the dust, and the golde of Ophir as the flyntes of the riuers
Yea almightie God his owne selfe shalbe thy defence, and thou shalt haue plentie of siluer
Then shalt thou haue thy delite in the almightie, and lift vp thy face vnto God
Then shalt thou make thy prayer vnto him, and he shall heare thee, and thou shalt kepe thy promises
Thou shalt also decree a thing, and he shall establishe it vnto thee, and the light shall shine in thy wayes
When [the wicked] be cast downe, thou shalt say, I am lifted vp: and God shall saue the humble person
The innocent shal deliuer the Ilande: it shalbe preserued by the purenesse of thyne handes
23: Though my talke be this day in bitternesse, and my plague greater then my groning
O that I might know him, and finde him, and that I might come before his seate
I woulde pleade my cause before hym, and fill my mouth with argumentes
I woulde knowe what aunswere he woulde geue me, and vnderstande what he woulde say vnto me
Will he pleade against me with his great power? No, but he will make me the stronger
There the righteous might dispute with him, so shoulde I be deliuered for euer from my iudge
Behold, though I go forwarde I find him not: If I go backwarde, I can get no knowledge of hym
If I go on the left side where he doth his worke, I can not attayne vnto him: Againe, if I go on the right side, he hydeth him selfe that I can not see hym
But as for my way, he knoweth it, and tryeth me, that as the gold I may come foorth
My foote doth kepe his path, his hie way haue I holden, and will not go out of it
I will not forsake the commaundement of his lippes, I haue esteemed the wordes of his mouth more then myne appoynted foode
He is still at one poynt, and who can turne him? he doth as him listeth, and bringeth to passe what he will
He perfourmeth the thing that is appoynted for me, and many such thinges doth he
This is the cause that I shrinke at his presence, so that when I consider him, I am afrayde of hym
For God maketh my heart softe, and the almightie putteth me in feare
Because I am not cut of before the darkenesse, neither hath he couered the cloude fro my face
24: Considering then that there is no time hyd from the almightie, how happeneth it that they which know him do not regarde his dayes
For some men remoue the landemarkes, robbe men of their cattell, and feede of the same
They driue away the asse of the fatherlesse, and take the wydowes oxe for a pledge
They cause the poore to turne out of the way, so that the poore of the earth hyde them selues together
Beholde, as wilde asses in the desert go they foorth to their worke, & ryse betimes to spoyle: Yea the very wildernesse ministreth foode for them & their children
They reape the corne fielde that is not their owne, and let the vineyarde of the vngodly alone
They cause the naked to lodge without garment, and without couering in the colde
They are wet with the showres of the mountaynes, and embrace the rocke for want of a couering
They plucke the fatherlesse from the brest, and take the pledge from the poore
They let hym go naked without clothing, and haue taken away the sheafe of the hungrie
The poore are fayne to labour in their oyle mylles, yea and to treade in their wyne presses, and yet to suffer thirst
Men out of the citie crye vnto the Lord with sighing, the soules of the slayne also crye out, yet God regardeth not their complaynt
Where as they are conuersaunt among them that abhorre the light, they know not his way, nor continue in his pathes
The murtherer ryseth early and killeth the poore and needy, and in the night is as a thiefe
The eye of the adulterer wayteth for the darkenesse, & sayth, There shall no eye see me: and disguiseth his face
In the darke they digge through houses, whiche they marked for them selues in the day time: they knowe not the light
The morning is to them euen as the shadow of death: if one know them, they are in the terrours of the shadowe of death
[The vngodly] is swyft vpon the water: their portion shalbe cursed in the earth, and he shall not beholde the way of the vineyardes
As the drye grounde and heate consume the snowye waters: so shall the graue the sinners
The pitifull man shall forget hym, he shalbe sweete to the wormes, he shalbe no more remembred, & his wickednesse shalbe broken as a tree
He hath oppressed the barren that can not beare, and vnto the wydow hath he done no good
He drue the mightie after hym with his power, and when he was gotten vp no man was sure of lyfe
And though they gaue him to be in safetie, yet his eyes are vpon their wayes
They are exalted for a litle, but [shortly] are gone, brought to pouertie, and taken out of the way, yea and vtterly pluckt of, as the eares of corne
Is it not so? Who will then reproue me as a lyer, and say that my wordes are nothing worth? Bildad proueth that no man is cleane nor without sinne before God
25: Then aunswered Bildad the Suhite, and sayde
Is there power and feare with him aboue, that maketh peace sitting in his hyghnesse
Is there any number of his armies, and vpon whom shal not his light arise
But how may a man compared vnto God, be iustified? or how can he be cleane that is borne of a woman
Beholde, the moone shyneth nothing in comparison to him, and the starres are vncleane in his sight
Howe much more then man that is but corruption, and the sonne of man which is but a worme
26: Who hast thou helped? Him that is without strength? sauest thou the arme that hath no strength
Where is the counsayle that thou shouldest geue him which hath no wisdome? Hast thou shewed the way of right lyuing
To whom hast thou spoken these wordes? who made the breath to come out of thy mouth
Are not dead thinges shapen vnder the waters, and thinges by the waters side
He is naked before him, and the very destruction it selfe can not be hyd out of his sight
He stretcheth out the noorth ouer the emptie place, and hangeth the earth vpon nothing
He byndeth the water in his cloudes, & the cloude is not broken vnder them
He holdeth backe the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloude before it
He hath compassed the waters with certayne boundes, vntill the day and night come to an ende
The very pillers of heauen tremble and quake at his reproofe
He stilleth the sea with his power, and through his wysdome smyteth he the strength therof
His spirite hath garnished the heauens, & his hand hath made the crooked serpent
Lo, this is now a short summe of his wayes: but howe litle a portion heare we of hym? who can vnderstande the thunder of his power
27: And Iob proceeded and went foorth in his parable, saying
As God lyueth whiche hath taken away my iudgement, and the almightie that hath vexed my minde
Whyle my breath is in me, and the winde that God hath geuen me is in my nostrels
My lippes shall talke of no vanitie, and my tongue shall speake no disceite
God forbyd that I should graunt your cause to be right: As for me, vntill myne end come will I neuer go fro myne innocentie
My righteous dealing kepe I fast, which I will not forsake: my heart shal not reproue me of my dayes
Therfore myne enemie shalbe founde as the vngodly, and he that taketh part against me, as the vnrighteous
For what hope hath the hypocrite though he haue great good, if God take away his soule
Will God heare his crye, when trouble commeth vpon him
Hath he such pleasure and delite in the almightie, that he dare alway call vpon God
I wil teache you in the name of God, and the thing of the almightie will I not kepe from you
Behold, all ye your selues haue seene it, why then do ye thus vanishe in vanitie
Saying: This is the portion that the wicked haue of God, and the heritage that tyrauntes shall receaue of the almightie
If he get many children, they shall perishe with the sworde, and his posteritie shall haue scarcenesse of bread
His remnaunt shalbe buried in death, and his widowes shall not weepe
Though he heape vp siluer as the dust, and prepare rayment as the clay
He may well prepare it, but the godly shall put it on, and the innocent shall deale out the money
He buyldeth his house as the moth, & as a booth that the watchman maketh
When the riche man sleepeth, he shall not be gathered [to his fathers,] they opened their eyes, and he was gone
Terrour taketh holde vpon hym as a water fludde, and the tempest stealeth him away in the night season
A vehement east winde caryeth him hence, and he departeth: a storme hurleth him out of his place
God shal cast vpon him, and not spare, though he woulde fayne flee out of his hande
Then clap men their handes at hym, and hisse at him out of his place
28: There is a place wher siluer is brought out of, and where golde is tryed
Where yron is digged out of the grounde, & stones resolued to metall
The darkenesse shall once come to an ende: he can seke out the grounde of all thinges, the stones, the darke, and the shadowe of death
He causeth the fluddes to breake out against the inhabitant, and the waters forgotten of the foote, beyng hygher then man, are gone away
Out of the same earth commeth bread, and vnder it as it were fire is turned vp
The stones of it are a place of Saphires, and the dust of it is golde
There is a way that the birdes knowe not, that no vultures eye hath seene
Wherin the lions whelpes walke not, and where no lion commeth
[There] putteth he his hande vpon the stonie rockes, and ouerthroweth the mountaynes by the rootes
Riuers flowe out of the rockes, & loke what is pleasaunt, his eye seeth it
He bindeth the fluddes that they do not ouerflow: and the thing that is hid bringeth he to light
Where then is wysdome founde? and where is the place of vnderstanding
Ueryly no man can tell howe worthy a thing she is, neither is she found in the lande of them that lyue
The deepe sayth, She is not in me: the sea sayth, She is not with me
She can not be gotten for golde, neither may the price of her be bought with any siluer
No wedges of gold of Ophir, no precious Onix stones, no Saphires may be valued with her
No, neither golde nor christall shall be equall vnto it, nor her exchaunge shalbe for the plate of fine golde
No mention shalbe made of Corall nor of the Gabis: for wisdome is more precious then pearles
The Topas of Ethiopia shall not be equall vnto it, neither shall it be valued with the wedge of pure golde
Whence then commeth wysdome? and where is the place of vnderstanding
She is hid from the eyes of all men liuing, yea & from the foules of the ayre
Destruction and death say, We haue hearde the fame therof with our eares
But God seeth her way, and knoweth her place
For he beholdeth the endes of the worlde, and loketh vpon all that is vnder heauen
When he wayed the windes and measured the waters
When he made a decree for the rayne, and a way for the lightninges of the thunder
Then dyd he see her, then declared he her, prepared her, and knewe her
And vnto man he sayd: To feare the Lorde is wysdome, and to forsake euyll is vnderstanding
29: So Iob proceeded and went foorth in his parable, saying
O that I were as I was in the monethes by past, and in the daies when God preserued me
When his light shined vpon my head, when I went after the same light and shining, euen through the darknesse
As it stoode with me when I was young, when God prospered my house
When the almightie was yet with me, when my children stoode about me
When my wayes ranne ouer with butter, and when the stonie rockes gaue me riuers of oyle
When I went out to the gate, euen to the iudgement seate, and when I prepared my seate in the streete
The young men saw me and hid them selues, and the aged arose, and stoode vp
The princes left of their talking, and layed their hand to their mouth
The mightie kept still their voyce, and their tongue cleaued to the roofe of their mouth
When the eare heard me, it blessed me: & when the eye sawe me, it gaue witnesse to me
For I deliuered the poore when he cryed, and the fatherlesse, and hym that had none to helpe hym
The blessing of him that was redy to perishe came vpon me, and I caused the widowes heart to reioyce
And why? I put vpon me righteousnesse, which couered me as a garment, and equitie was my crowne
I was an eye to the blinde, and a foote to the lame
I was a father to the poore: and when I knewe not the cause, I sought it out diligently
I brake the iawes of the vnrighteous man, and pluckt the spoyle out of his teeth
Then I sayde, I shall die in my nest: and I shall multiplie my dayes as the sande
For my roote was spread out by the waterside: and the deawe lay vpon my corne
Myne honour encreased more and more, & my bow was euer the stronger in my hande
Unto me men gaue eare, me they regarded, and with scilence they taried for my counsell
After my woordes they replied not, and my talke dropped vpon them
They wayted for me as for the raine: and gaped vpon me, as [the grounde doeth to receaue] the latter shoure
When I laughed, they beleued it not, & the light of my countenaunce would they not put out
When I agreed vnto their way, I was the chiefe, and sate as a king with his armie about him: and when they were in heauinesse, I was their comfortour
30: But nowe they that are younger then I haue me in derision: yea euen they whose fathers I would haue thought scorne to haue set with the dogges of my cattell
For wherto might the strength of their handes haue serued me? for the time was but lost among them
For very miserie and hunger they fled into the wildernesse, a darke place, horrible and waste
Plucking vp nettles among the busshes, and the iuniper rootes for their meate
And when they were dryuen foorth, men cryed after them as it had ben afafter a thiefe
Their dwelling was in the cleftes of brookes, yea in the caues and dennes of the earth
Among the busshes went they about crying, and vnder the thornes they gathered them selues together
They were the children of fooles and vyllaynes, which are more vile then the earth
Now am I their song, & am become their yesting stocke
They abhorre me and flee farre from me, and stayne my face with spittle
Because God hath loosed my corde and humbled me, they haue loosed the bridle before me
Upon my right hande ryse the young men against me, they haue hurt my feete, treading vpon me as vpon the wayes of their destruction
My pathes haue they cleane marred, it was so easye for them to do me harme, that they needed no man to help them
They fell vpon me, as it had ben the breaking in of waters, and came in by heapes to destroy me
Feare is turned vpon me, and they pursue my soule as the wind, and my health passeth away as a cloude
Therfore is my soule now powred out vpon me, and the dayes of my trouble haue taken hold vpon me
My bones are pearsed through in the night season, and my sinewes take no rest
For the vehemencie of sorowe is my garment chaunged, whiche compasseth me about as the coller of my coote
He hath cast me into the myre, and I am become like asshes and dust
When I crie vnto thee, thou doest not heare me: and though I stande before thee, yet thou regardest me not
Thou art become myne enemie, and with thy violent hande thou takest part against me
[In times past] thou diddest set me vp on hye, to be caried as it were aboue the wynde, [but nowe] hast thou geuen me a very sore fall
Sure I am that thou wilt bryng me vnto death, euen to the lodging that is due vnto all men liuing
Notwithstanding, thou wilt not stretch out thyne hand against him that is in the graue: shal men crie out against him that is in destruction
Dyd not I weepe with hym that was in trouble? Had not my soule compassion vpon the poore
Yet neuerthelesse, where as I loked for good, euyll came vnto me: & where I wayted for light, there came darkenesse
My bowels seethe in me without rest, for the dayes of my trouble are come vpon me
I went mourning without heate, I stoode vp in the congregation, & communed with them
But nowe I am a brother of dragons, and a felowe of Estriches
My skinne vpon me is [turned] to blacke, and my bones are brent with heate
My harpe is turned to mourning, and my organs into the voyce of them that weepe
31: I made a couenaunt with myne eyes: why then should I loke vpon a mayden
For how great a portion shall I haue of God? and what inheritaunce from the almightie on hye
Is not destruction to the wicked? and straunge punishement to the workers of iniquitie
Doth not he see my wayes, and tell all my goynges
If I haue walked in vanitie, or if my feete haue runne to disceaue
Let me be wayed in an euen balaunce, that God may see myne innocencie
If my steppe hath turned out of the way, & myne heart walked after myne eyes, and if any blot haue cleaued to my handes
Then shall I sowe, and an other eate: yea my posteritie shalbe cleane rooted out
If my heart haue ben deceaued by a woman, or if I haue layde wayte at my neyghbours doore
Then let my wife grinde vnto an other man, and let other men lye with her
For this is a wickednesse, and sinne that is worthy to be punished
Yea a fire that vtterly should consume and roote out all my increase
If I euer thought scorne to do right vnto my seruauntes & maydens, when they had any matter against me
When God will sit in iudgement, what shall I do? & when he will visite me, what aunswere shal I geue him
He that fashioned me in my mothers wombe, made he not him also? were we not both shapen a like in our mothers bodies
If I denied the poore of their desire, or haue caused the eyes of the wydow to wayte in vayne
If I haue eaten my morsell alone, that ye fatherlesse hath not eaten therof
(For from my youth it hath growen vp with me as with a father, and from my mothers wombe I haue ben guyde to the [wydowe]
If I haue seene any perishe for want of clothing, or any poore for lake of rayment
If his loynes haue not blessed me, because he was warmed with the fleece of my sheepe
If I haue lift vp mine hand against the fatherlesse, when I sawe that I might helpe him in the gate
Then let myne arme fall fro my shoulder, and myne arme holes be broken from the bone
For I haue euer feared the vengeaunce and punishment of God, and [knewe very well that] I was not able to beare his burthen
Haue I put my trust in golde? or haue I sayde to the wedge of golde, thou art my confidence
Haue I reioyced because my power was great, and because my hande gat so much
Dyd I euer greatly regarde the rysing of the sunne? or had I the goyng downe of the moone in great reputation
Hath my heart medled priuyly with any disceite? or did I euer kisse myne owne hande
(That were a wickednesse worthy to be punished: for then shoulde I haue denyed the God that is aboue.
Haue I euer reioyced at the hurt of myne enemie? or was I euer glad that any harme happened vnto him? [Oh, no.
I neuer suffred my mouth to sinne, by wishing a curse to his soule
Dyd not the men of myne owne housholde say, Who shall let vs to haue our belly full of his fleshe
The straunger dyd not lodge in the streete, but I opened my doores vnto him that went by the way
Haue I kept secrete my sinne, and hyd myne iniquitie, as Adam dyd
Though I coulde haue made afeard a great multitude, yet the most contemptible of the families dyd feare me: so I kept scilence, and went not out of the doore
O that I had one which woulde heare me: beholde my signe in the whiche the almightie shal aunswere for me, though he that is my contrarie partie hath written a booke against me
Yet will I take it vpon my shoulder, & as a garlande binde it about my head
I will tell hym the number of my goinges, & go vnto him as to a prince
But if case be that my lande crye against me, or that the forowes thereof make any complaynt
If I haue eaten the fruites therof vnpayed for, yea if I haue greeued the soules of the maisters therof
Then let thystles growe in steede of my wheate, and cockle for my barlye
32: So these three men ceassed to aunswere Iob, because he held him selfe a righteous man
But Elihu the sonne of Barachel the Buzite, of the kinred of Ram, was very sore displeased at Iob, because he called hym selfe iust before God
And with Iobs three friendes he was angry also, because they had founde no reasonable aunswere, and yet condempned Iob
Nowe taried Elihu, till they had ended their comunication with Iob: for why? they were elder then he
So when Elihu sawe that these three men were not able to make Iob aunswere, he was miscontent
Therfore Elihu the sonne of Barachel the Buzite aunswered, and sayde: [Considering that] I am young, and ye be men of age, I was afrayde, and durst not shewe foorth my mynde
For I thought thus within my selfe: It becommeth old men to speake, and the aged to teache wysdome
Euery man no doubt hath a mynde, but it is the inspiration of the almightie that geueth vnderstanding
Great men are not alway wyse, neither doth euery aged man vnderstande the thing that is lawfull
Therefore I say, heare me, and I wil shewe you also myne vnderstanding
For when I had wayted till ye made an end of your talking, and hearde your wysdome, what argumentes ye made in your communication
Yea when I had diligently pondred what ye sayde, I found not one of you that made any good argument against Iob, that directly could make aunswere vnto his wordes
Lest ye should say: We haue found out wisdome, God shall cast hym downe, and no man
He hath not spoken vnto me, and I wil not aunswere hym as ye haue done
For they were so abashed, that they coulde not make aunswere, nor speake one worde
When I had wayted (for they spake not, but stoode still and aunswered no more:
Then aunswered I in my turne, and I shewed myne opinion
For I am full of matter, and the spirite within me compelleth me
Beholde, my belly is as the wine, whiche hath no vent, lyke the newe bottels that bruste
[Therfore] will I speake, that I may haue a bent: I will open my lippes, and make aunswere
I will regarde no maner of person, no man will I spare
For if I woulde go about to please men, I knowe not howe soone my maker would take me away
33: Wherefore heare my wordes O Iob, and hearken vnto all that I will say
Behold, I haue now opened my mouth, my tongue hath spoken in my throte
My heart doth order my wordes aright, and my lippes talke of pure wysedome
The spirite of God hath made me, and the breath of the almightie hath geuen me my lyfe
If thou canst then geue me aunswere, prepare thy selfe and stande before me face to face
Beholde, before God I am euen as thou: for I am fashioned & made euen of the same molde
Beholde, my terrour shall not feare thee, neither shall my hande be heauy vpon thee
Now hast thou spoken in myne eares, & I haue heard the voyce of thy wordes
I am cleane without any fault, I am innocent, & there is no wickednesse in me
But lo, he hath piked a quarell against me, and taketh me for his enemie
He hath put my foote in the stockes, and looketh narowlye vnto all my pathes
Behold, in this hast thou not done right, I wil make aunswere vnto thee, that God is greater then man
And why doest thou then striue against him? for he shall not geue the accomptes of all his wordes
For God speaketh once or twise, and yet man vnderstandeth it not
In dreames and visions of the night, when slumbring commeth vpon men that they fall asleepe in their beddes
He roundeth them in the eares, and sealeth their correction
That he may withdrawe man from euyll enterprises, and deliuer hym from pride
And kepe his soule from the graue, and his life from the sworde
He chasteneth hym with sickenesse vpon his bedde, he layeth sore punishement vpon his bones
So that his lyfe may away with no bread, and his soule abhorreth to eate any dayntie meate
In so much that his body is cleane consumed away, and his bones appeare which before were not seene
His soule draweth vnto the graue, and his lyfe to death
Now yf there be a messenger, one among a thousande, sent for to speake vnto man, and to shew him the right way
Then the Lord is mercifull vnto him, and sayth, He shalbe deliuered, that he fall not downe to the graue: for I am sufficiently reconciled
Then shal his fleshe be as freshe as a childes, and shal returne as in the dayes of his youth
He shall pray vnto God, and he will be fauorable vnto him, and he shall see his face with ioy, for he will render vnto man his righteousnesse
A respect hath he vnto men, let man then say, I haue offended, I did vnrighteously, & it hath done me no good
Yea he hath deliuered my soule from destruction, and my lyfe shall see the light
Lo all these worketh God alway with man
That he bring backe his soule from the graue to the light, yea the light of the lyuing
Marke wel O Iob, and heare me: hold thee still, and I will speake
But if thou hast any thing to say, then aunswere me, and speake: for I desire to iustifie thee
If thou hast nothing, then heare me, and hold thy tongue, and I shall teache thee wysdome
34: Elihu proceeding in his aunswere, sayde
Heare my wordes O ye wise men, hearken vnto me ye that haue vnderstanding
For the eare discerneth wordes, and the mouth tasteth the meates
As for iudgement, let vs seke it out among our selues, that we may knowe what is good
[And why?] Iob hath sayd, I am righteous, and God hath taken away my iudgement
In my right I shoulde be a lyer: my wounde is incurable without my fault
Where is there such a one as Iob, that drinketh vp scornefulnesse like water
Which goeth in the companie of wicked doers, and walketh with vngodly men
For he hath sayde, It profiteth a man nothing that he shoulde walke with God
Therfore hearken vnto me ye that haue vnderstanding: farre be it from God that he shoulde meddle with wickednesse, & farre be it from the almightie that he shoulde meddle with vnrighteous dealing
For he shall rewarde man after his workes, and cause euery man to finde according to his wayes
Sure it is that God wil not do wickedly, neither wyll the almightie paruert iudgement
Who ruleth the earth but he? or who hath placed the whole world
If he set his heart vpon [man] and gather vnto hym selfe his spirite and his breath
All fleshe shall come to naught at once, and all men shall turne againe vnto dust
If thou nowe haue vnderstanding, heare what I say, and hearken to the voyce of my wordes
May he be a ruler that loueth not right? or may he that is a very innocent man do vngodly
Is it reason that thou shouldest say to the king, Thou art wicked, or thou art vngodly, and that before the princes
God hath no respect vnto the persons of the lordly, and regardeth not the riche more then the poore: for they be al the worke of his handes
In the twinckling of an eye shall they dye, and at midnight when the people and the tirantes rage, then shall they perishe, & be taken away without handes
For his eyes loke vpon the wayes of man, and he seeth all his goinges
There is no darkenesse nor shadowe of death that can hide the wicked doers from him
For God wil not lay vpon man more then he hath sinned, that he should enter into iudgement with him
He shall destroy the mightie without seeking, and shall set other in their steede
Therefore shall he declare their workes: he shall turne the night, and they shalbe destroyed
The vngodly doth he punishe openly
Because they tourned backe from him, and would not consider all his wayes
Insomuch that they haue caused the voyce of the poore to come vnto him, and now he heareth the complaint of such as are in trouble
When he geueth quietnesse, who can make trouble? and when he hydeth his face, who can beholde him? whether it be vpon nations, or vpo one man onely
Because the hypocrite doth raigne, because the people are snared
Surely of God onely it can be saide, I haue pardoned, I wyll not destroy
If I haue gone amisse, enfourme thou me: If I haue done wrong, I wyll leaue of
Wyll he perfourme the thing through thee? for thou hast reproued his iudgement, thou also hast thyne owne minde, and not I: But speake on what thou knowest
Let men of vnderstanding tell me, and let a wyse man hearken vnto me
Iob hath not spoken of knowledge, neither were his wordes according to wysdome
O father, let Iob be well tryed, because he hath aunswered for wicked men
Yea aboue his sinne he doth wickedly, triumpheth among vs, and multiplieth his wordes against God
35: Thinkest thou it right that thou sayest, I am more righteous then God
