For thou sayest: what aduauntage wyll it be vnto thee, and what profite shall I haue of my sinne
Therefore wyll I geue aunswere vnto thee, aud to thy companions with thee
Loke vnto the heauen and beholde it, consider the cloudes which are hyer then thou
If thou hast sinned, what hast thou done against him? If thyne offences be many, what hast thou done vnto him
If thou be righteous, what geuest thou him? or what wyll he receaue of thyne hande
Thy wickednesse [may hurt] a man as thou art, and thy righteousnesse [may profite] the sonne of man
They which are oppressed crye out vpon the multitude, yea they crye out for the power of the mightie
But none sayth, Where is God that made me? and that geueth vs occasion to praise him in the night
Which teacheth vs more the the beastes of the earth, and geueth vs more wysdome then the foules of heauen
If any such complaine, no man geueth aunswere, and that because of the wickednesse of proude tirauntes
For God wyll not heare vanitie, neither wyll the almightie regarde it
Although thou sayest [to God] thou wylt not regarde it: yet iudgement is before him, trust thou in him
But now because his anger hath not visited, neither called men to accompt with great extremitie
Therefore doth Iob open his mouth but in vaine, & he maketh many wordes without knowledge
36: Elihu also proceeded, and saide
Holde thee still a litle, & I shall shew thee what I haue yet to speake on gods behalfe
I wyll open vnto thee yet farre higher knowledge, and wil ascribe righteousnesse vnto my maker
And truely my wordes shall not be vaine, seeing he is with thee that is perfect in knowledge
Beholde, the great God casteth away no man, for he him selfe is mightie in power and wysdome
As for the vngodly he shall not preserue him, but shall helpe the poore to their right
He shal not turne his eyes away from the righteous, but as kinges shal they be in their throne, he shal stablish them for euer, and they shalbe exalted
But if they be layde in chaynes, or bounde with the bondes of trouble
Then wyll he shew them their worke, & their sinnes which haue ouercome them
He with punishing and nurturing of them, roundeth them in the eares, warneth them to leaue of from their wickednesse, and to amende
If they now wyll take heede & serue him, they shal weare out their dayes in prosperitie, and their yeres in pleasure
But if they wil not hearken, they shal go through the sworde, and perishe or euer they be aware
As for hypocrites in heart, they shall heape vp wrath [for them selues] for they call not vpon him, though they be his prisoners
Thus shal their soule perishe in foolishnes, and their lyfe among the fornicatours
The poore shall he deliuer out of his affliction, and rounde them in the eare when they be in trouble
Euen so would he take thee out of the straite place, into a brode place in the which there is no straitnes: yea, & make thy table quiet replenished with fatnesse
Neuerthelesse, thou hast commended the iudgement of the vngodly, and euen such a iudgement & sentence shalt thou suffer
And seeing there is wrath with God, beware lest he take thee away in thy wealth, & all that thou hast to redeeme thee can not deliuer thee
Thinkest thou that he wyll regarde thy riches? he shall not care for golde, nor for all them that excell in strength
Spend not the night in carefull thoughtes, how he destroyeth some, and bringeth other in their place
But beware that thou turne not aside to wickednesse and sinne, which hitherto thou hast chosen more then affliction
Beholde, God is of a mightie hie power: Where is there such a guide and lawe geuer as he
Who wyll reproue him of his way? Who wil say vnto him, Thou hast done wrong
Remember that thou do magnifie his worke which men do praise
All men see it, yea men do beholde it a farre of
Beholde, so great is God that he passeth our knowledge, neither can the number of his yeres be searched out
Sometime he restrayneth the rayne, and againe he sendeth rayne by his cloudes
Which rayne the cloudes do droppe, and let fall aboundantly vpon men
Who can consider the spreadinges out of his cloudes, the coueringes of his tabernacle
Behold, he doth stretch his light vpon it, and couereth the bottome of the sea
For by these gouerneth he his people, and geueth them aboundance of meate
With the cloudes he hydeth the light, and at his commaundement it breaketh out
Which dashing vpon the next cloudes, shew tokens of wrath
37: At this also my heart is astonied, and moued out of his place
Heare then the sounde of his voyce, & the noyse that goeth out of his mouth
He directeth it vnder the whole heauen, and his light vnto the endes of the worlde
A roring voyce foloweth it: for his glorious maiestie geueth a thuder clappe, & he will not stay whe his voyce is heard
God thundreth marueylously with his voyce, great thinges doth he which we can not comprehend
He commaundeth the snow, and it falleth vpon earth: he geueth the rayne a charge, and the showres haue their strength and fall downe
With the force of the rayne he shutteth men vp, that all men may knowe his workes
The beastes creepe into their dennes, and remaine in their places
Out of the south commeth the tempest, and colde out from the north winde
At the breath of God the hoare frost is geuen, and the brode waters are frosen
He maketh the cloudes to labour in geuing moystnesse, and againe with his light he dryueth away the cloude
He turneth the heauens about by his gouernement, that they may do whatsoeuer he commaundeth them vpon the whole worlde
Whether it be for punishment, or for his lande, or to do good to them that seeke him
Hearken vnto this O Iob, stand still, and consider the wonderous workes of God
Didst thou know when God disposed them? & caused the light of his cloudes to shine
Hast thou knowen the varietie of the cloudes, and the wonderous workes of him which is perfect in knowledge
And how thy clothes are warme, when the lande is stil through the south winde
Hast thou helped him to spreade out the heauens which are strong and bright as a loking glasse
Teache vs what we shall saye vnto him: for we are vnmeete to frame our talke because of darkenesse
Shall it be tolde him what I saye? Shall man speake when he shalbe destroyed
For men see not the light that shineth in the cloudes: but the winde passeth and cleanseth them
The faire weather commeth out of the north, the prayse thereof is to God who is terrible
It is the almightie, we can not finde him out: he is excellent in power and iudgement, and aboundaunt in iustice: he afflicteth not
Let men therefore feare him: for there shall no man see him that is wyse in his owne conceit
38: Then aunswered the Lorde vnto Iob out of the whirle winde, and saide
What is he that darkeneth his counsaile by wordes without knowledge
Girde vp thy loynes lyke a man: for I wyl question with thee, see thou geue me a direct aunswere
Where wast thou when I layed the foundations of the earth? Tell playnely, if thou hast vnderstanding
Who hath measured it, knowest thou? or who hath spread the lyne vpon it
Whereupon are the foundations set? or who layed the corner stone thereof
Where wast thou when the morning starres praysed me together, and all the children of God reioyced triumphantly
Who shut the sea with doores, when it brake foorth as out of the wombe
When I made the cloudes [to be] a covering for it, and swadled it with the darke
When I gaue it my commaundement, making doores and barres for it
Saying, Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shalt thou laye downe thy proude and hie waues
Hast thou geue the morning his charge since thy dayes, and shewed the day spring his place
That it might take holde of the corners of the earth, and that the vngodly might be shaken out of it
They are fashioned as is the clay with the seale, and all stand vp as a garment
The vngodly shall be disapointed of their light, and the arme of the proude shalbe broken
Camest thou euer into the grounde of the sea, or walkedst in the lowe corners of the deepe
Haue the gates of death ben opened vnto thee? or hast thou seene the doores of the shadowe of death
Hast thou also perceaued how brode the earth is? If thou hast knowledge of all this
Then shewe me the way where light dwelleth, & where is the place of darkenesse
That thou shouldest receaue it in the boundes thereof, and know the pathes to their houses
Knewest thou afore thou wast borne how olde thou shouldest be
Wentest thou euer into the treasures of the snow, or hast thou seene the secrete places of the hayle
Which I haue prepared against the time of trouble, against the time of battaile and warre
By what way is the light parted? and into what land breaketh the east winde
Who deuideth the waters into diuers chanels? or who maketh a way for the lightening and thunder
To cause it to rayne on the earth where no man is, and in the wildernesse where none inhabiteth
To satisfie the desolate and waste grounde, and to cause the budde of the hearbe to spring foorth
Who is the father of the rayne? or who hath begotten the droppes of the deawe
Out of whose wombe came the yce? Who hath gendred the coldnesse of the ayre
That the waters are hidde as [with] a stone, and lye congealed aboue the deepe
Wylt thou hinder the sweete influences of the seuen starres? or loose the bandes of Orion
Canst thou bring foorth Mazzaroth in their time? canst thou also guide Arctutus with his sonnes
Knowest thou the course of heauen, that thou mayest set vp the ordinaunce thereof vpon the earth
Moreouer, canst thou lift vp thy voyce to the cloudes, that they may powre downe a great rayne vpon thee
Canst thou send the lightninges also, that they may go their way, and be obedient vnto thee, saying, Lo here are we
Who hath put wysdome in the reynes? or who hath geuen the heart vnderstanding
Who numbreth the cloudes in wysdome? who stilleth the vehement waters of the heauen
To cause the earth to grow into hardnesse, & the clots to cleaue fast together
Wylt thou hunt the pray for the lion? or fill the appetite of the lions whelpes
When they couche in their places, and tarie in the couert to lye in wayte
Who prouideth meate for the rauen, when his young ones crye vnto God, and flee about for lacke of meate
39: Knowest thou the time whe the wylde goates bring foorth their young among the stonye rockes? or layest thou wayte when the hindes vse to calue
Canst thou number the monethes that they go with young? or knowest thou the time when they bring foorth
They lye downe, they calue their young ones, and they are deliuered of their trauaile and paine
Yet their young ones grow vp, and waxe fatte through good feeding with corne: They go foorth, and returne not againe vnto them
Who letteth the wylde asse to go free? or who looseth the bondes of the wylde mule
Euen I which haue geuen the wyldernesse to be their house, and the vntilled land to be their dwelling
They force not for the multitude of people in the citie, neither regarde the crying of the driuer
But seeke their pasture about the mountaines, and folowe the greene grasse
Wyll the vnicorne do thee seruice, or abide still by thy cribbe
Canst thou binde the yoke about the vnicorne in the forowe, to make him plowe after thee in the valleyes
Mayst thou trust him because he is strong, or commit thy labour vnto him
Mayst thou beleue him that he wyll bring home thy corne, or carry any thing vnto thy barne
Gauest thou the faire winges vnto the pecockes, or winges and fethers vnto the Estriche
For she leaueth her egges in the earth, and heateth them in the dust
She remembreth not that they might be troden with feete, or broken with some wilde beaste
So harde is she vnto her young ones as though they were not hers, and laboureth in vaine without any feare
And that because God hath taken wysdome from her, & hath not geuen her vnderstanding
When her time is that she fleeth vp on hie, she careth neither for the horse nor the ryder
Hast thou geue the horse his strength, or learned him to ney coragiously
Canst thou make him afrayde as a grashopper? where as the stoute neying that he maketh is fearefull
He breaketh the grounde with the hooffes of his feete, he reioyceth cherefully in his strength, and runneth to meete the harnest men
He layeth aside all feare, his stomacke is not abated, neither starteth he backe for any sworde
Though the quiuers rattle vpon him, though the speare and shielde glister
Yet rusheth he in fiercely beating the grounde, he thinketh it not the noyse of the trumpettes
But when the trumpettes make most noyse, he saith, tushe, for he smelleth the battaile a farre of, the noyse of the captaines and the shouting
Commeth it through thy wysdome that the Goshauke flieth toward the south
Doth the Egle mount vp, and make his nest on hye at thy comaundement
He abydeth in stony rockes, and dwelleth vpon the hye toppes of moutaines
From whence he seeketh his praye, and loketh farre about with his eyes
His young ones also sucke vp blood: and where any dead body lyeth, there is he
40: Moreouer the Lorde spake vnto Iob, and saide
Shall he whom the almightie wyl chasten, contend with him? Should not he which disputeth with God, geue him an aunswere
Then Iob aunswered the Lorde, saying
Beholde, I am vyle, what shall I aunswere thee, [therefore] I wyll laye my hande vpon my mouth
Once haue I spoken, but I wyll saye no more: yea twyse, but I wyl proceede no further
Then aunswered the Lorde vnto Iob out of the whirle winde, and saide
Girde vp thy loynes now lyke a man: I wyll demaunde of thee, and make thou aunswere
Wylt thou disanul my iudgement? or wylt thou condempne me, that thou mayst be righteous
Is thy power then lyke the power of God? maketh thy voyce a sounde as his doth
Decke thy selfe now with excellencie and maiestie, and araye thy selfe with beautie and glory
Cast abrode the indignation of thy wrath, and beholde euery one that is proude, and abase him
Loke on euery one that is arrogant, and bring him lowe, & destroy the wicked in their place
Hide them in the dust together, and couer their faces in secrete
Then wyll I confesse vnto thee also, that thyne owne right hande shall saue thee
Beholde the beaste Behemoth, who I made with thee, which eateth haye as an oxe
Lo how his strength is in his loynes, and what power he hath in the nauil of his body
When he wyll, he spreadeth out his tayle lyke a Cedar tree, all his sinowes are stiffe
His bones are lyke pipes of brasse, yea his bones are lyke staues of iron
He is the chiefe of the wayes of God, he that made him wyl make his sword to approche vnto him
Surely the mountaines bring him foorth grasse, where all the beastes of the fielde take their pastime
He resteth him in the shade, in the couerte of the reede and fennes
The trees couer him with their shadowe, and the wyllowes of the brooke compasse him about
Beholde, he drinketh vp whole ryuers and feareth not, he thinketh that he can drawe vp Iordane into his mouth
He taketh it with his eyes, and yet the hunter putteth a bridle into his nose
41: Canst thou drawe out Leuiathan with an hooke, or binde his tongue with a corde
Canst thou put a hooke in the nose of him, or bore his iawe through with a naule
Wyl he make many faire wordes with thee [thinkest thou] or flatter thee
Wyll he make a couenaunt with thee? or wilt thou take him for a seruaunt for euer
Wylt thou take thy pastime with him as with a birde, wilt thou binde him for thy maydens
That thy companions may make a refection of him: or shall he be parted among the marchauntes
Canst thou fil the basket with his skin? or the fishe panier with his head
Laye thyne hande vpon him, remember the battaile, and do no more so
Beholde his hope is in vaine: for shall not one perishe euen at the sight of him
No man is so fierce that dare stirre him vp: Who is able to stande before me
Or who hath geuen me any thyng aforehande, that I may rewarde him againe? All thinges vnder heauen are myne
I wyll not keepe secrete his great strength, his power, nor his comely proportion
Who can discouer the face of his garment? or who shall come to him with a double brydle
Who shall open the doores of his face? for he hath horrible teeth round about
His scales are as it were strong shieldes, so fastened together as if they were sealed
One is so ioyned to another, that no ayre can come in
Yea, one hangeth so vpon another, & sticketh so together, that they can not be sundred
His neesinges make a glistering like fyre, and his eyes lyke the morning shine
Out of his mouth go torches, and sparkes of fire leape out
And out of his nostrels there goeth a smoke, lyke as out of an hotte seething pot, or caldron
His breath maketh the coles burne, and the flambe goeth out of his mouth
In his necke ther remaineth strength, and nothing is to labourous for him
The members of his body are ioyned [so strait one to another,] and cleaue so fast together, that he cannot be moued
His heart is as hard as a stone, and as fast as the stythie that the smyth smiteth vpon
When he goeth the mightie are afraide, and feare troubleth them
If any man drawe out a sword at him, it shall not hurt him: there may neither speare, laueling, nor brestplate abide him
He setteth asmuch by iron as by a strawe, and asmuch by brasse as by a rotten sticke
He starteth not away from him that bendeth the bowe: & as for sling stones he careth asmuch for stouble as for the
He counteth the dartes no better then a strawe, he laugheth him to scorne that shaketh the speare
Sharpe stones are vnder him lyke potsheardes, and he lyeth vpon sharpe thinges as vpon the soft myre
He maketh the deepe to boyle lyke a pot, and stirreth the sea together lyke an oyntment
He maketh the path to be seene after him, and he maketh the deepe to seeme all hoarie
Upon earth there is no power lyke vnto his: for he is so made that he feareth not
He beholdeth all the hye thinges, he is a king ouer all the children of pride
42: Then Iob aunswered the Lord, and saide
I know that thou hast power ouer all thinges, and that there is no thought hid vnto thee
For who can keepe his owne counsaile so secrete but it shalbe knowen? Therefore haue I spoken that I vnderstoode not, euen the thinges that are to wonderfull for me, and passe myne vnderstanding
O hearken thou vnto me also, and let me speake: aunswere vnto the thing that I wyll aske thee
I haue heard of thee by the hearing of the eare, but nowe myne eye seeth thee
Wherefore I geue myne owne selfe the blame, and take repentaunce in the dust and asshes

Now when the Lorde had spoken these wordes vnto Iob, it came to passe that the Lorde saide to Eliphas the Themanite: I am displeased with thee, and thy two friendes: for ye haue not spoken of me the thyng that is right, lyke as my seruaunt Iob hath done

Therefore take you now seuen oxen, and seuen rammes, and go to my seruaunt Iob, and offer vp for your selues a burnt offring, and my seruaunt Iob shall pray for you: him wyll I accept, and not deale with you after your foolishnesse, in that ye haue not spoken of me the thing which is right, lyke as my seruaunt Iob hath done
So Eliphas the Themanite, and Bildad the Suhite, and Sophar the Naamathite, went and did according as the Lorde commaunded them: the Lorde also accepted the person of Iob
And the Lorde tourned the captiuitie of Iob when he prayed for his friendes: Yea the Lorde gaue Iob twyse as much as he had afore

And then came there vnto him all his brethren, all his sisters, and all they that had ben of his acquaintaunce afore, and did eate bread with him in his house, and had compassion on him, and comforted him ouer all trouble that the Lorde had brought vpon him: euery man also gaue him a certaine summe of money, and a iewell of golde
So the Lorde blessed the last dayes of Iob more then the first: for he had fourteene thousand sheepe, sixe thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses
He had seuen sonnes also, and three daughters
The first daughter called he Iemima, the second Kezia, and the third Kerenhapuch
In al the land were no women found so faire as the daughters of Iob: and their father gaue them inheritaunce among their brethren
After this liued Iob an hundred and fourtie yeres: so that he sawe his children, and his childrens children into the fourth generation
And so Iob dyed, being olde, and of a perfect age
